nameStory: Creeping woodsorrel gets its name from its low, sprawling growth habit that spreads along the ground rather than standing upright. The 'woodsorrel' part comes from its sour-tasting leaves, which contain oxalic acid - the same compound that gives rhubarb its tartness. Some people also call it 'sleeping beauty' because its delicate leaves fold up at night or when touched, as if going to sleep.
description: Creeping woodsorrel is a delicate, low-growing plant that hugs the ground with its spreading stems. It's a small herbaceous plant that rarely grows more than a few inches tall, instead forming mats that creep outward. The distinctive three-leaflet leaves look like tiny shamrocks, and small bright yellow flowers peek up from the foliage. This somewhat fragile-looking plant is tougher than it appears and thrives in moist conditions throughout New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three heart-shaped leaflets arranged like a shamrock, soft to the touch and folding closed when disturbed or at nightfall. The leaflets have a fresh, lemony scent when crushed and taste pleasantly sour.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers with five delicate petals, about the size of your pinky nail. They sit on thin stalks above the leaves and have a papery texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeps along the ground on thin, trailing stems that root at the joints where they touch soil. Forms low mats rather than growing upright, staying close to the earth.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender, pointed seed pods that stand upright like tiny green horns. When ripe, they split open with a satisfying 'pop' and shoot seeds several feet away.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, weak stems that feel soft and slightly succulent between your fingers. They're often reddish or purplish, especially where they meet the leaf stalks.

habitat: Look for creeping woodsorrel in moist, partially shaded areas like garden beds, lawn edges, and disturbed soil around buildings. It thrives in rich, well-watered soil and is commonly found as a garden 'weed' in flower beds and vegetable patches. You'll often spot it growing between stepping stones, along building foundations, or in any spot that stays consistently damp.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as tiny shamrock-like leaves, with the first small yellow flowers appearing in late spring. The fresh green foliage is at its most tender and sour-tasting.
seasonality.summer: Actively blooming with bright yellow flowers and producing the characteristic horn-shaped seed pods. This is when the plant spreads most actively, with stems rooting wherever they touch moist soil.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until the first frost, with mature seed pods popping open to disperse seeds. The leaves may take on reddish tints as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely in cold areas, surviving as seeds and underground parts. In milder microclimates, some leaves may persist through winter looking wilted but remaining green.

funFact: The seed pods are natural catapults - when they ripen, they explosively split open and can launch seeds up to 10 feet away with an audible 'pop' sound that you can actually hear if you're quiet and close enough!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with upright yellow woodsorrel, but remember 'creeping' stays low while 'upright' stands tall - if you can walk on it without bending over, it's probably the creeping type. The growth habit is the easiest way to tell them apart since both have identical shamrock leaves and yellow flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite looking like a delicate shamrock, this isn't related to true clovers at all - it's in the woodsorrel family. Many gardeners consider it a persistent weed because of its ability to spread quickly and pop up everywhere, but it's actually edible and makes a tangy addition to salads in small amounts.
compareHints: Creeping woodsorrel differs from its upright cousin (Oxalis stricta) mainly in its prostrate, mat-forming growth habit versus the upright's tall, erect stems. Unlike the white-flowered mountain woodsorrel found in New England's forests, this species has yellow flowers and prefers disturbed, sunny to partially shaded spots. The creeping habit and preference for garden settings make it the most likely woodsorrel you'll encounter around homes and cultivated areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mountain woodsorrel differs from its yellow-flowered relatives in the genus by having white petals with pink veins instead of bright yellow ones.
Among New England's woodsorrels, upright yellow woodsorrel stands tall while creeping woodsorrel sprawls flat along the ground.
Slender yellow woodsorrel is smaller and more delicate than upright yellow woodsorrel, with thinner stems that tend to sprawl rather than stand erect.
Violet wood-sorrel is easily distinguished from its New England relatives by its purple flowers - all other common wood-sorrels in the region have yellow flowers.
Unlike other woodsorrels in New England which have green leaves and yellow flowers, false shamrock stands out with its deep maroon foliage and white or pink blooms.
Among New England's woodsorrels, this is the only one with large pink flowers - all the others have either small yellow blooms or purple ones.
Great yellow woodsorrel differs from its more common relatives like upright yellow woodsorrel and slender yellow woodsorrel by its significantly larger leaflets and more spreading growth habit.
Pink-sorrel stands out from New England's other woodsorrels primarily by its pink flowers - most relatives have yellow blooms, while violet woodsorrel has purple flowers.
